intro: Three Gs fall to E♭, and Beethoven stops the clock with a fermata. From that tiny opening he builds a movement of horn calls, whispered exchanges and one unaccompanied oboe, before the orchestra drives home C minor.

sections.mNote: E♭ major; the four-note rhythm continues in the bass

cues.title: Three Gs, then silence
cues.text: A quaver rest, three Gs, then E♭ held under a fermata. Three Fs follow, falling to an even longer D. Beethoven gives the conductor two chances to suspend the beat before the movement has properly begun.
cues.evidence: Beethoven, Symphony No. 5, I, bars 1–5; Mutopia 941, first-violin and cello parts. The second held note occupies two bars.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: The horns open a door
cues.text: The horns turn the opening rhythm into a broad call: B♭–B♭–B♭, then E♭, F and a lower B♭. The intervals widen, and E♭ major offers a little room to breathe.
cues.evidence: Symphony No. 5, I, bars 59–62; Mutopia 941, horn part. Written G–G–G–C–D–G for horns in E♭ sounds B♭–B♭–B♭–E♭–F–B♭.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: A song above the rhythm
cues.text: The first violins begin a sweet E♭-major melody, marked dolce. Under it, the cellos keep returning to three short B♭s and a longer E♭. The opening rhythm has slipped into the accompaniment.
cues.evidence: Symphony No. 5, I, bars 63–70; Mutopia 941, first-violin and cello parts. Cello figures in bars 65–66 and 69–70.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: An evening at the theatre
cues.text: Vienna, 22 December 1808: the audience at the Theater an der Wien hears this symphony for the first time. The same programme includes the Sixth Symphony, Fourth Piano Concerto and Choral Fantasy. Beethoven gives them an extraordinary amount of new music in one evening.
cues.evidence: Première date, venue and concert programme documented by Eastman School of Music: https://www.esm.rochester.edu/beethoven/symphony-no-5/.

cues.title: Back to the first G
cues.text: Two silent bars lead back to the opening. The whole exposition repeats: the fierce C-minor music, the horn call, the E♭-major song. Each tune gets a second hearing before Beethoven begins to break it apart.
cues.evidence: Symphony No. 5, I, repeat enclosing bars 1–124; two bars of rests at 123–124. Mutopia 941 orchestral parts; second performed occurrence of bar 1.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Fate at the door
cues.text: In 1840, thirteen years after Beethoven’s death, his former secretary Anton Schindler reports that Beethoven described the opening bars to him: “Thus Fate knocks at the door!” Schindler also forged entries in Beethoven’s conversation books, and historians have long doubted his word.
cues.evidence: Anton Schindler, Biographie von Ludwig van Beethoven (Münster, 1840), p. 241: “So pocht das Schicksal an die Pforte!” https://archive.org/details/biographievonlud00schi. Schindler’s forged conversation-book entries were exposed by Peter Stadlen, “Schindler’s Beethoven Forgeries”, The Musical Times 118 (July 1977), 549–52; summary in BBC Music Magazine, https://www.classical-music.com/features/composers/beethovens-conversation-books. The motto is also discussed by the Eastman School of Music: https://www.esm.rochester.edu/beethoven/symphony-no-5/

cues.title: The horns change direction
cues.text: After the second E♭-major ending, the horns call again, this time falling to G. The strings answer with three D♭s falling to C. The old rhythm now brings a sharp clash: D♭ against the horns’ held G.
cues.evidence: Symphony No. 5, I, bars 125–128; Mutopia 941, horns, strings and bassoons. Horn call begins on sounding B♭; strings enter on D♭ in bar 126.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: One chord answers another
cues.text: The quick rhythm has dwindled to single chords. Winds and strings answer across gaps, getting quieter. The violins move through B♭, C♭ and D♭ before dropping to low C♯. There is scarcely a tune left, yet the waiting is intense.
cues.evidence: Symphony No. 5, I, bars 210–221; Mutopia 941, first violin and wind parts, with diminuendo, sempre più piano and pp.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: The oboe speaks alone
cues.text: The orchestra stops on a G-major chord. One oboe keeps its G, then descends through F, E♭ and D in a little Adagio. A turn curls around the line. For a few seconds, one player has the whole movement to themselves.
cues.evidence: Symphony No. 5, I, bar 268; Mutopia 941, oboe part: G fermata, Adagio descent, E♭–D–C–D turn and final D fermata. The strings rest after their chord.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: The bassoons inherit the call
cues.text: The bassoons take the call that belonged to the horns. Their G–G–G, C, D, G leads to the violin song in C major. The melody is a minor third lower than before, and its new companions give it a warmer voice.
cues.evidence: Symphony No. 5, I, bars 303–310; Mutopia 941, bassoons and first violin. Comparison with the horn call and violin melody in bars 59–66.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Horns that could not
cues.text: In the exposition the horns call in E♭ major. In the recapitulation the same call falls in C major, and Beethoven gives it to the bassoons, since the E♭ horns would have had to change to C crooks. The milder bassoons weaken the solution that the major key seemed to promise.
cues.evidence: Eastman School of Music, Beethoven site, Symphony No. 5: in the recapitulation Beethoven uses “the milder-toned bassoons” for the horn call rather than ask the E♭ horns to change to C crooks. https://www.esm.rochester.edu/beethoven/symphony-no-5/ Horn and bassoon parts at bars 59–62 and 303–306: Mutopia 941.

cues.title: High C, changing ground
cues.text: The violins hold and repeat a high C while the bass moves C–A♭–E–F. The same top note belongs to changing chords beneath it. This is a long coda, with more arguments still to come before the final C-minor chords.
cues.evidence: Symphony No. 5, I, bars 374–381, first violin and cello; final C-minor chords in bars 491–502. Mutopia 941.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: The first hold returns
cues.text: Near the end the opening’s held E♭ returns under a fermata. Three Fs fall to a long D, as they did in the first five bars. Beethoven stops the pulse once more with the same unequal holds.
cues.evidence: Symphony No. 5, I, bars 479–483 compared with bars 2–5; Mutopia 941, first-violin and cello parts: E♭ with fermata, then F–F–F and D tied across two bars.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

transitions.title: A pause leaves the horns alone
transitions.from: A · Three Gs and a fermata
transitions.to: B · Horn call and violin song
transitions.how: A diminished-seventh chord over C cuts off, followed by a silent bar. A short B♭-major chord over D points towards E♭ major. The horns fill the cleared space with three B♭s, then E♭, F and B♭. Their held note carries into the quiet violin melody, marked dolce.
transitions.evidence: Symphony No. 5, I, bars 56–67; Mutopia 941, strings, oboes, bassoons and horns. Bar 56: A–C–E♭–G♭; bar 57: rests; bar 58: B♭ major over D; bars 59–62: horn call.

transitions.title: Two silent bars reset the opening
transitions.from: B · Horn call and violin song
transitions.to: A · The opening and horn call repeat
transitions.how: Three short dominant chords resolve to E♭ major: the bass moves B♭–E♭ and the first violins D–E♭. Two silent bars follow. The repeat brings back the opening Gs and held E♭, with the strings and clarinets playing in octaves. The broad closing chord has narrowed to a single line.
transitions.evidence: Symphony No. 5, I, bars 121–124 followed by bars 1–2, second occurrence. Mutopia 941 orchestral parts: cadence, two bars of rests and opening octave line.

transitions.title: D♭ clashes with a held G
transitions.from: A · The opening and horn call repeat
transitions.to: Dev · Fragments pass between winds and strings
transitions.how: The E♭-major cadence and two silent bars return. This time the horns play B♭–B♭–B♭ down to G. The strings answer D♭–D♭–D♭–C against that held G, briefly forming a tritone. After the fermata, quiet second violins and bassoons introduce F minor over the cellos’ C.
transitions.evidence: Symphony No. 5, I, bars 121–124, second occurrence, and 125–130. Mutopia 941: horn call, D♭–C string response and F–A♭–C harmony in bar 130.

transitions.title: Two chords become one
transitions.from: Dev · Fragments pass between winds and strings
transitions.to: Dev · Fragments pass between winds and strings
transitions.how: Winds and strings exchange pairs of slow chords. The strings answer with C seventh over G, then F minor over A♭. Soon each reply contains only one chord, with a rest while the other group speaks. A diminuendo leads towards pianissimo F♯ minor; the repeated quavers have disappeared.
transitions.evidence: Symphony No. 5, I, bars 196–220. Mutopia 941 string and wind parts: C7/G and F minor/A♭ at 198–199, single-chord exchanges from 209 and F♯ minor at 215–220.

transitions.title: Fragments recover the opening rhythm
transitions.from: Dev · Fragments pass between winds and strings
transitions.to: A′ · The opening returns with wind reinforcements
transitions.how: Quiet winds and strings trade B–D–F–A♭, the diminished seventh that points towards C minor. Fortissimo A♭–A♭–A♭–F fragments break into those exchanges and crowd closer together. The bass moves from F to three Gs; the opening E♭ arrives under its fermata, now reinforced by winds and horns.
transitions.evidence: Symphony No. 5, I, bars 233–253; Mutopia 941 strings, oboes, bassoons and horns. Diminished-seventh exchanges at 233–240, compressed A♭–F figures and return at 248.

transitions.title: A half cadence becomes an oboe solo
transitions.from: A′ · The opening returns with wind reinforcements
transitions.to: A′ · The opening returns with wind reinforcements
transitions.how: The orchestra reaches G major, a half cadence in C minor. The strings stop, leaving the oboe on G. Its unaccompanied Adagio descends F–E♭–D, turns through E♭–D–C–D and descends again. A fermata holds the final D before the violins resume their three A♭s falling to F.
transitions.evidence: Symphony No. 5, I, bars 268–270; Mutopia 941, oboe and string parts. The entire Adagio cadenza belongs to bar 268.

transitions.title: Bassoons lead the song into C
transitions.from: A′ · The opening returns with wind reinforcements
transitions.to: B′ · Bassoon call and C-major song
transitions.how: A silent bar precedes a G-major chord over B, the dominant of C. Bassoons take the call: G–G–G–C–D–G. Their final G continues beneath the quiet violin melody, now beginning G–C–B–C. The exposition’s horn call and E♭-major song have returned in C major, a minor third lower.
transitions.evidence: Symphony No. 5, I, bars 301–310; Mutopia 941, bassoon and string parts. Compare bars 57–66.

transitions.title: The closing chord starts another argument
transitions.from: B′ · Bassoon call and C-major song
transitions.to: Coda · High C over a shifting bass
transitions.how: G major resolves to C major, with G–C in the bass and B–C in the first violins. That arrival also begins the coda. High C alternates between held notes and tremolo while the bass moves C–A♭–E–F. Beneath the repeated C, the chords change from C major to F minor and back.
transitions.evidence: Symphony No. 5, I, bars 373–381; Mutopia 941, first violin, second violin, viola and cello. C major, F minor/A♭, C major/E and F minor occupy successive two-bar spans.

source.title: Beethoven, Symphony No. 5, I, Mutopia 941, from the Breitkopf & Härtel parts

timeline.note: Clarinets and strings strike the opening in octaves, holding E♭ under the fermata.
The strings pass the four-note rhythm upwards above held bassoon notes.
Winds, brass and timpani join the strings for the forceful chords and repeated notes.
The strings climb; oboes, clarinets and horns answer their short phrases.
The orchestra gathers into repeated chords before the pause and horn call.
The horns play alone: three B♭s, then E♭, F and a lower B♭.
The violins sing the E♭-major melody. Clarinets and bassoons answer; flutes and oboes join later.
Falling violin figures lead towards the cadence, with trumpets and timpani reinforcing the chords.
The repeat restores the opening Gs in clarinets and strings.
The strings trade the rhythm again above sustained bassoons.
Trumpets and timpani rejoin the strings and woodwind for the repeated orchestral outburst.
The climbing string phrases draw answers from woodwind and horns.
A crescendo fills the orchestra before the horn call’s second appearance.
The horns call towards E♭ major again, alone after the orchestral pause.
The violins repeat their sweet melody above the lower strings’ repeated notes.
The full orchestra closes the repeated exposition in E♭ major, followed by two silent bars.
Horns and clarinets start the development’s call; the strings answer D♭–D♭–D♭–C.
Quiet strings and bassoons establish F minor; fragments pass through the clarinets and horns.
The horns repeat the short-note rhythm while orchestral chords alternate with string runs.
Wind and brass pairs of slow chords receive answers from the strings.
The replies shrink to single chords, passed between winds and strings at pianissimo.
Diminished-seventh chords alternate between groups before the repeated-note rhythm breaks back in.
The opening returns with winds, brass and timpani reinforcing the strings.
Quiet string phrases leave space for the woodwind, with the oboe carrying a sustained line.
A G-major chord reaches a fermata; the horns rest.
One oboe plays the unaccompanied Adagio, descending through F, E♭ and D.
The violins restart the repeated A♭s; wind and brass answers follow.
The full orchestra builds towards the pause before the bassoon call.
The bassoons take the call alone: G–G–G–C–D–G.
The violins sing in C major, with woodwind replies and quiet timpani.
Trumpets and timpani reinforce the returning closing chords.
Violins and upper winds sustain high C while the bass changes C–A♭–E–F.
Fortissimo orchestral chords alternate with the strings’ short figures.
Quiet woodwind and violin phrases hover above held low strings.
The whole orchestra alternates G-major and C-minor chords before the final C.

composer.epithet: He could make a symphony out of four notes, and spent his last years finding things four string players had never said.
facts: Neefe in Bonn; Haydn, Albrechtsberger and Salieri in Vienna
Bonn until 1792; Vienna and its surrounding villages for the rest of his life
Nine symphonies · five numbered piano concertos · 32 numbered piano sonatas · 16 string quartets · Fidelio
Described his hearing loss in 1801; used conversation books from 1818

quote.text: I live only in my notes.
quote.source: Beethoven to Franz Gerhard Wegeler, Vienna, 29 June 1801; our translation

composer.background:
In March 1778 Johann van Beethoven advertised a concert in Cologne by his six-year-old son. Ludwig was seven. His father, a singer in the electoral chapel at Bonn, hoped to launch another child prodigy; his grandfather, also Ludwig, had risen from singer to Kapellmeister in the same establishment. The boy was baptised on 17 December 1770, probably the day after his birth. Music was the family trade. By his teens he was playing the organ for services and the viola in the court orchestra, learning operas from the middle of the string section.

Christian Gottlob Neefe put Bach’s Well-Tempered Clavier before him and helped him into paid employment. The Breuning household supplied books, friendship and a refuge from Johann’s drinking. After his mother died in 1787, Beethoven increasingly supported his younger brothers. In November 1792 the elector sent him to Vienna to study with Haydn. He was supposed to come back. French troops occupied Bonn in 1794, and the court that paid him disappeared.
